mcqs.question: A device inspects each incoming frame's destination MAC address and forwards it only out the port that device is known to sit on. What is this device, and at which layer does it operate?
options: A hub, operating at the physical layer
A router, operating at the network layer
A repeater, operating at the transport layer
A switch, operating at the data link layer
mcqs.explanation: Reading MAC addresses to make a per-port forwarding decision is exactly a data-link-layer switch's job. A hub does no addressing at all (it just repeats), a router works on IP addresses at layer 3, and a repeater/transport-layer combination isn't a real device pairing.

mcqs.question: Why do almost all modern LANs use a physical star topology instead of bus or ring?
options: A single failed cable or device in a star only isolates that one node, while a break in bus or ring can disrupt the whole shared segment
Star topology uses less cable overall than bus or ring
Star topology was mandated by the IEEE 802.3 Ethernet standard as the only legal wiring
Bus and ring topologies cannot support more than two devices
mcqs.explanation: Fault isolation is the real reason: star wiring through a central switch means one bad cable takes down one device, not the segment. Star typically uses more cable, not less (the less-cable claim is false); Ethernet doesn't mandate topology (the IEEE-mandate claim); and bus/ring historically supported many devices (the two-device-limit claim is false).

mcqs.question: You replace a hub with a switch on a busy LAN segment. What changes, and what stays the same?
options: Both collisions and broadcast flooding disappear, since switches eliminate all shared-medium behavior
Collisions disappear (each switch port is its own collision domain), but broadcast frames still flood every port — the broadcast domain is unchanged
Broadcast flooding disappears, but collisions remain exactly as before
Nothing changes — switches and hubs behave identically at layer 2
mcqs.explanation: A switch gives each port its own collision domain, eliminating collisions, but it still floods broadcast frames to every port just like a hub would — only a router or VLAN segmentation splits a broadcast domain. This is the exact distinction the concept is testing: switches fix collisions, not broadcast scope.
